results.name: last_minus_first_example_proximity
results.description: Yes-rate for non-example targets within 5 of the LAST shown example minus within 5 of the FIRST shown example (targets near both excluded, multi-example sets only); the model is order-blind so its null is ~0, a positive observed value means a recency effect, negative a primacy effect the model lacks.
results.code:
# name: last_minus_first_example_proximity
# description: Yes-rate for non-example targets within 5 of the LAST shown example minus within 5 of the FIRST shown example (targets near both excluded, multi-example sets only); the model is order-blind so its null is ~0, a positive observed value means a recency effect, negative a primacy effect the model lacks.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    n = ex.notna().sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    first = ex.iloc[:, 0].values
    last = ex.values[np.arange(len(ex)), n.values - 1]
    is_ex = ex.eq(df["target"].astype(int), axis=0).any(axis=1).values
    df_ = np.abs(t - first)
    dl = np.abs(t - last)
    base = (n.values >= 2) & (~is_ex)
    near_last = base & (dl <= 5) & (df_ > 5)
    near_first = base & (df_ <= 5) & (dl > 5)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    if near_last.sum() == 0 or near_first.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near_last].mean() - r[near_first].mean())

results.name: upward_minus_downward_extension
results.description: Yes-rate for targets 1-20 above the set maximum minus yes-rate for targets 1-20 below the set minimum (multi-example sets); the model's intervals are symmetric (up to edge effects), so observed above the null means people extend generalization upward more than downward than the model predicts, below means downward more.
results.code:
# name: upward_minus_downward_extension
# description: Yes-rate for targets 1-20 above the set maximum minus yes-rate for targets 1-20 below the set minimum (multi-example sets); the model's intervals are symmetric (up to edge effects), so observed above the null means people extend generalization upward more than downward than the model predicts, below means downward more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    n = ex.notna().sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    lo, hi = ex.min(axis=1), ex.max(axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    up = (n >= 2) & (t > hi) & (t <= hi + 20)
    dn = (n >= 2) & (t < lo) & (t >= lo - 20)
    if up.sum() == 0 or dn.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[up].mean() - r[dn].mean())

results.name: set_size_yes_slope
results.description: OLS slope of yes-rate on number of examples (2-4) for non-example targets; observed more negative than the null means people tighten generalization with more examples faster than the model's size principle/noise rate predicts, less negative means slower.
results.code:
# name: set_size_yes_slope
# description: OLS slope of yes-rate on number of examples (2-4) for non-example targets; observed more negative than the null means people tighten generalization with more examples faster than the model's size principle/noise rate predicts, less negative means slower.
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].str.count(",") + 1
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    is_ex = ex.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    m = (~is_ex) & (n >= 2)
    x = n[m].astype(float).values
    y = df.loc[m, "rating"].astype(float).values
    if len(x) < 3 or np.var(x) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.cov(x, y, bias=True)[0, 1] / np.var(x))

results.name: shared_tens_digit_outside_yes
results.description: Among non-example targets outside the example range and not sharing a last digit with any example, yes-rate when the target shares its tens digit (decade) with some example minus when it does not; observed above the null means people use decade similarity more than the model's digit rules/intervals produce, below means less.
results.code:
# name: shared_tens_digit_outside_yes
# description: Among non-example targets outside the example range and not sharing a last digit with any example, yes-rate when the target shares its tens digit (decade) with some example minus when it does not; observed above the null means people use decade similarity more than the model's digit rules/intervals produce, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    tens_ex = (ex // 10)
    last_ex = ex % 10
    shares_tens = tens_ex.eq(t // 10, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    shares_last = last_ex.eq(t % 10, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    lo, hi = ex.min(axis=1), ex.max(axis=1)
    outside = (t < lo) | (t > hi)
    base = outside & ~shares_last
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    a = base & shares_tens
    b = base & ~shares_tens
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: isolated_example_neighbourhood_yes
results.description: Among 3-4 example sets, yes-rate for non-example targets within 6 of the most isolated example (largest nearest-neighbour gap, >=15) minus yes-rate for targets within 6 of the other examples; observed below the null means people discount an outlying example (treat it as noise) more than the inferred noise rate allows, above means they generalize around it more.
results.code:
# name: isolated_example_neighbourhood_yes
# description: Among 3-4 example sets, yes-rate for non-example targets within 6 of the most isolated example (largest nearest-neighbour gap, >=15) minus yes-rate for targets within 6 of the other examples; observed below the null means people discount an outlying example (treat it as noise) more than the inferred noise rate allows, above means they generalize around it more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values.astype(float)
    d = np.abs(ex[:, :, None] - ex[:, None, :])
    k = ex.shape[1]
    d[:, np.arange(k), np.arange(k)] = np.inf
    d = np.where(np.isnan(d), np.inf, d)
    nn = d.min(axis=2)
    nn = np.where(np.isnan(ex), -1, nn)
    iso = nn.argmax(axis=1)
    gap = nn.max(axis=1)
    rows = np.arange(len(t))
    iso_val = ex[rows, iso]
    dist = np.abs(ex - t[:, None])
    is_ex = np.nansum(dist == 0, axis=1) > 0
    near_iso = np.abs(t - iso_val) <= 6
    other = dist.copy()
    other[rows, iso] = np.inf
    other = np.where(np.isnan(other), np.inf, other)
    near_other = other.min(axis=1) <= 6
    base = (n >= 3) & (gap >= 15) & (~is_ex)
    a = base & near_iso & ~near_other
    b = base & near_other & ~near_iso
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: ruleless_set_inside_range_yes
results.description: Yes-rate for non-example targets strictly inside the example range, for 2-4 example sets with no common rule (gcd 1, mixed parity, no shared last digit, no shared digit); observed above the null means people fill in the range of patternless sets more than the model (which can treat examples as noise), below means less.
results.code:
# name: ruleless_set_inside_range_yes
# description: Yes-rate for non-example targets strictly inside the example range, for 2-4 example sets with no common rule (gcd 1, mixed parity, no shared last digit, no shared digit); observed above the null means people fill in the range of patternless sets more than the model (which can treat examples as noise), below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    n = ex.notna().sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    exi = ex.fillna(0).astype(int).values
    g = np.gcd.reduce(exi, axis=1)
    valid = ex.notna().values
    par = np.where(valid, exi % 2, -1)
    mixed = (par == 0).any(axis=1) & (par == 1).any(axis=1)
    last = np.where(valid, exi % 10, -1)
    shared_last = np.all((last == last[:, [0]]) | ~valid, axis=1)
    shared_digit = np.zeros(len(df), dtype=bool)
    for dgt in range(10):
        has = (exi % 10 == dgt) | ((exi // 10) % 10 == dgt) & (exi >= 10) | ((exi == 100) & (dgt in (0, 1)))
        shared_digit |= np.all(has | ~valid, axis=1)
    ruleless = (n.values >= 2) & (g == 1) & mixed & ~shared_last & ~shared_digit
    lo, hi = ex.min(axis=1), ex.max(axis=1)
    is_ex = ex.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    m = ruleless & (t > lo).values & (t < hi).values & ~is_ex.values
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].astype(float).values[m].mean())

results.name: round_number_target_bias
results.description: For sets containing no multiple of 10, yes-rate for non-example targets that are multiples of 10 minus yes-rate for other non-example targets; observed above the null means people over-endorse round numbers relative to the model, below means they under-endorse them.
results.code:
# name: round_number_target_bias
# description: For sets containing no multiple of 10, yes-rate for non-example targets that are multiples of 10 minus yes-rate for other non-example targets; observed above the null means people over-endorse round numbers relative to the model, below means they under-endorse them.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    has10 = (ex % 10 == 0).any(axis=1)
    is_ex = ex.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    base = (~has10) & (~is_ex)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    a = base & (t % 10 == 0)
    b = base & (t % 10 != 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: within_set_response_spread
results.description: Mean (over sets with >=10 trials) of the within-set variance of yes/no responses p(1-p); observed above the model's null means people discriminate targets within a set less sharply (more uniform/graded) than predicted, below means they are more all-or-none per set than the model.
